questions.topic: The pivot chord that enables a modulation
questions.learningObjective: identify the pivot chord that carries a modulation from one key to another
questions.stem: A chorale in c major reaches the chord A3-C4-E4 sounding together, holds it for one bar, and then continues F3-A3-C4-F4 and G3-B3-D4-G4. Which chord role makes the change of key possible, and why?

options.text: A pivot chord, since A3-C4-E4 is diatonic in c major and also the tonic of a minor, so one chord reads in both keys
A passing chord, since the a minor triad only connects the two chords and the new key arrives with the following f major triad
options.misconception: treats a chord that belongs to two keys as a mere link between two chords

options.text: A secondary dominant, since A3-C4-E4 tonicises a minor and so the chorale has modulated to its dominant
options.misconception: reads a diatonic common chord as a chord that applies a dominant to a new key

options.text: An appoggiatura chord, since the a minor triad is really a decorated tonic that delays the arrival of the real tonic
options.misconception: mistakes a fully diatonic triad for a decoration of a single key

questions.explanation: The whole of the work is done by one chord carrying two readings at once. A3-C4-E4 is built on the fifth degree of c major, so it is the mediant there and belongs to that key without any alteration. The same three pitch classes are the tonic of a minor, so once the following chord settles onto F3-A3-C3-F4 and then G3-B3-D4-G4 the ear has to read a minor, and the chord that could have been read either way is what made the switch audible rather than abrupt. A secondary dominant would be a chord with a raised third, something like C3-E3-G3-B3 tonicising d minor, and a passing chord is a non-chord tone that leans on a neighbour. Neither describes a triad that is equally at home in two keys. The trap is to think a modulation needs a special chord; what it needs is a chord that is not special at all, but ambiguous.
questions.hint: Ask whether the chord is diatonic in both keys at once, and what each key would call it.

questions.topic: Measuring a close modulation by its tonic distance
questions.learningObjective: compute the distance in semitones between the tonics of two closely related keys
questions.stem: A passage leaves c minor for its relative major, e-flat major, and the modulation is complete. Counting semitones upward from c to e-flat, how far apart are the two tonics?
questions.explanation: Up from c the notes run c to c-sharp for one, d for two and e-flat for three, so the two tonics lie three semitones apart. The second route is to go the other way and read the distance as a minor sixth: descending from c, b is one, b-flat is two, a is three, a-flat is four, g is five and e-flat is six, and a minor sixth and a minor third are two names for the same three semitones. Three semitones is what makes these keys close relatives rather than distant ones, and it is the reason the change of key can be made by respelling a note instead of rewriting the melody. The trap is to answer four, which would be a major third and would describe a chromatic mediant relation rather than a relative major.
questions.hint: Count up from c a semitone at a time, and check by counting down to the same note.

questions.topic: A common-tone modulation and the pitch it retains
questions.learningObjective: explain what a common-tone modulation retains and what has to change
questions.stem: A piece moves from f major to f minor without changing its tonic, so the bass keeps the note F2 throughout. What makes this a common-tone modulation, and what must be altered?

options.text: It is a common-tone modulation because f is held throughout as the common pitch, while three notes of the scale are lowered to reach the minor mode
It is a common-tone modulation because both keys share the same key signature, so no note at all has to be altered to change mode
options.misconception: believes the major and minor forms of a key share one signature

options.text: It is a modulation at all, because a change of mode on the same tonic is a change of colour rather than a change of key
options.misconception: denies that a move between relative modes counts as a modulation

options.text: It is a common-tone modulation because the three altered notes are the ones held over from the major form, so the common tones are the altered ones
options.misconception: names the altered notes as the retained common tones

questions.explanation: A common-tone modulation keeps one pitch sounding as the bridge while the rest of the collection is re-specified around it, and here the bridge is the tonic f itself, held in the bass from bar to bar. Reaching f minor from f major means lowering a to a-flat, d to d-flat and e to e-flat, three changes, while f, g, b-flat and c stay exactly as they were, so four of the seven notes never move. That leaves only three alterations, which is why this kind of modulation sounds smooth and why it is so common between movements and between the sections of a large piece. The trap is the key signature: f major has one flat and f minor has four, so the two keys do not share a signature and three notes genuinely do change. The second trap is the direction of the common tone; the notes that are held are the unaltered ones, not the altered ones.
questions.hint: Count how many of the seven scale notes have to move, and check which notes are shared.

questions.topic: Counting the pitch classes a common-tone modulation retains
questions.learningObjective: count the pitch classes two keys of the same tonic share
questions.stem: A modulation carries f major into f minor. F major holds f, g, a, b-flat, c, d and e; f minor holds f, g, a-flat, b-flat, c, d-flat and e-flat. How many of the seven notes are common to both collections?
questions.explanation: Reading across the two lists, f, g, b-flat and c appear in both, so four notes are retained. The second route starts from the changes instead of the retentions: three of the major notes have to move, a to a-flat, d to d-flat and e to e-flat, and seven less three leaves four. The four retained notes are enough to hold the two modes together, and the three that move are exactly the notes that give the minor its darker colour, since they are the lowered third, sixth and seventh degrees. The trap is to answer three, which counts the altered notes instead of the retained ones, or seven, which would mean the two modes share everything.
questions.hint: Either list the notes that appear in both, or subtract the altered notes from seven.

questions.topic: The distance between chromatic mediant keys
questions.learningObjective: state how a chromatic mediant key relates to the key it left
questions.stem: A slow movement leaves c major and settles without warning into a major, whose tonic a is a major third above the c. What makes a chromatic mediant different from an ordinary closely related key such as g major or a minor?

options.text: The new tonic is a third away from the old one rather than a fourth or fifth, so no note of the new key is diatonic and the change of key has to be spelled note by note
The new tonic is a third away, but because a third is diatonic in both keys a pivot chord can still carry the modulation as smoothly as it would in g major
options.misconception: believes a third-related key still shares a diatonic pivot chord

options.text: The new tonic is a third away, which is why the new key always has one more flat or one fewer sharp than the key it left
options.misconception: confuses the direction of the change with a change in signature size

options.text: The new tonic is a third away, so the modulation can only be achieved by a sudden change of key rather than by any prepared chord or respelled note
options.misconception: assumes a third-related modulation cannot be prepared at all

questions.explanation: Ordinarily related keys are a fourth or a fifth apart, and a fourth or a fifth apart means they share a great deal: g major and c major have six of seven notes in common, and a minor and c major have all seven. Those relationships are why a pivot chord exists at all. A chromatic mediant is a third away, which is a much more violent relationship, and in the c to a case the two keys share no notes whatever, since c major holds c, d, e, f, g, a and b while a major holds a, b, c-sharp, d, e, f-sharp and g-sharp. The overlap is one note name, a, and even that is a different note, a natural against a sharp. So a chromatic mediant cannot be reached by reinterpretation of a single chord; it has to be established by respelling and by a cadence in the new key, which is why the effect is so often used to darken a passage rather than to settle it.
questions.hint: Compare the note lists of the two keys and see whether any chord survives the move.

questions.topic: Sizing the gap between the tonics of a chromatic mediant pair
questions.learningObjective: compute the semitone distance between two chromatic mediant tonics
questions.stem: A modulation carries c major to a major, so the new tonic lies a major third above the old one or a minor sixth below it. Counting semitones from c up to a, how wide is that gap?
questions.explanation: Up from c, c-sharp is one, d is two, d-sharp is three, e is four, f is five, f-sharp is six, g is seven, g-sharp is eight and a is nine, so a lies nine semitones above c. The second route reads the same distance downward, where a minor sixth is nine semitones: c down to b is one, b-flat two, a three, a-flat four, g five, f six, e seven, e-flat eight and e-flat's octave a... counting properly, c down to a is a minor sixth, and a minor sixth is nine semitones, which agrees with the count upward. Nine semitones being neither a fourth nor a fifth is exactly why a major and c major are chromatic mediant partners and not ordinary related keys. The trap is four, which is a major third counted from c and lands on e, not on a.
questions.hint: Count upward a semitone at a time, and confirm the answer is also a minor sixth.

questions.topic: Reinterpreting a chord enharmonically
questions.learningObjective: explain how respelling lets one sounding chord serve two different functions
questions.stem: In c major a chord sounds g4, b4, d5 and f5. The composer then writes those same four sounds as g-sharp4, b4, d5 and f5, and the chord becomes the leading-note diminished seventh of a minor. What has changed, and what has not?

options.text: The sounding pitches have not changed at all, but the spelling has reassigned the root, so the chord's seventh is now read as a seventh rather than as a minor seventh above g
The sounding pitches have all been raised by a semitone, and the new spelling simply records the change in tuning
options.misconception: mistakes an enharmonic respelling for a change of pitch

options.text: The sounding pitches have not changed, but the chord has gained a new chord member, since four notes now stand where there were three
options.misconception: invents an extra chord member out of a change of notation

options.text: The sounding pitches have changed and the function has changed, because a diminished seventh cannot be spelled with a natural in it
options.misconception: believes a diminished seventh chord is barred from using a natural sign

questions.explanation: Nothing that a listener hears has moved. G natural and g-sharp are the same key on a piano, so the four sounding pitches and the bass beneath them are untouched by the respelling. What the spelling changes is the job the chord is doing. Spelled g, b, d, f the chord is a dominant seventh on g with a minor seventh above its root, and that reading puts it in c major as the chord on the dominant. Respelled g-sharp, b, d, f the same four pitches stack as three minor thirds above g-sharp, so the root has moved up a semitone in the notation and the interval from that new root to f is a diminished seventh rather than a minor seventh. Diminished sevenths are built to resolve outward, and respelling is what lets a chord that was functioning as a dominant become the leading-note chord of a key a semitone away. The trap is to think a respelling is a retuning, which would be a change of pitch rather than a change of name.
questions.hint: Separate what a listener hears from what the notes are called, and ask which of those changed.

questions.topic: Telling a German augmented sixth from an Italian one
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the German and Italian augmented sixth chords by their notes
questions.stem: Two predominant chords in c major are spelled a-flat3, c4, f-sharp4 and a-flat3, c4, e-flat4, f-sharp4. Which is the German sixth, and what is the extra note?

options.text: The four-note chord is the German sixth, and the extra note is e-flat4, the third of the tonic, added above the Italian's a-flat3, c4, f-sharp4
The four-note chord is the Italian sixth, and the extra note is e-flat4, so the Italian is the fuller of the two chords
options.misconception: reverses which of the two augmented sixth types carries the extra note

options.text: The three-note chord is the German sixth, and the German is the one that omits the third of the tonic to keep the chord in three parts
options.misconception: believes the smaller chord is the German type

options.text: Both are German sixths, since the German and Italian differ only in whether the chord resolves to the tonic or to the dominant
options.misconception: reduces the difference between the two types to their destination

questions.explanation: Both chords share a-flat3 and f-sharp4, which is the augmented sixth that gives the family its name and which expands outward a semitone at each end onto g3, the dominant. The Italian stops there, three notes only, and its directness is part of its character. The German adds e-flat4, the third of the tonic, so it is a four-note chord and it contains a perfect fifth from a-flat up to e-flat, a fifth that has to be handled carefully in the voice leading because it sits between the two notes that are about to move. The French type would instead insert d4, the second degree, giving a-flat3, c4, d4, f-sharp4. The trap is to assume the larger chord is the simpler one; in this family the three-note chord is the plainer of the two and the four-note chord is the one that creates extra work.
questions.hint: Compare the two note lists and identify which single pitch one chord has and the other lacks.

questions.topic: Sizing the augmented sixth that names the chord family
questions.learningObjective: compute the size in semitones of an augmented sixth between two stated notes
questions.stem: An Italian augmented sixth in c major is spelled a-flat3, c4 and f-sharp4. Counting semitones from a-flat3 up to f-sharp4, how wide is the interval between the outer notes?
questions.explanation: Up from a-flat, a-natural is one, b-flat two, b three, c four, c-sharp five, d six, e-flat seven, e eight, f nine and f-sharp ten, so the augmented sixth is ten semitones wide. The second route builds it from the interval it widens: a major sixth is nine semitones, and the word augmented means one semitone wider, so nine plus one is ten. Ten semitones is also the point of the chord, because the outer notes then expand outward to an octave on the dominant, a-flat3 falling a semitone to g3 while f-sharp4 rises a semitone to g4, and ten semitones of augmented sixth is what becomes twelve of octave. The trap is nine, which is a plain major sixth and would leave the upper note a whole tone too low to reach the dominant.
questions.hint: Count up a semitone at a time, or start from a major sixth and widen it by one.

questions.topic: Sizing the augmented fourth inside a German sixth
questions.learningObjective: compute the size in semitones of the augmented fourth inside a German sixth
questions.stem: A German augmented sixth in c major is spelled a-flat3, c4, e-flat4 and f-sharp4. The chord contains an augmented fourth between its inner two notes a step apart in the score. Counting semitones from c4 up to f-sharp4, how wide is that interval?
questions.explanation: Up from c, c-sharp is one, d two, d-sharp three, e four, f five and f-sharp six, so c4 up to f-sharp4 is six semitones, the tritone. The second route builds it the other way round: a perfect fourth is five semitones, and the sharp on the upper note widens it by one, so five plus one is six. Six semitones matters here because that interval, unlike a perfect fifth, does not want to stay put, and the f-sharp4 is one of the two notes that must rise a semitone onto g4 while a-flat3 falls onto g3. The trap is five, which is a perfect fourth and would be what the interval measured if the f-sharp carried a natural instead of a sharp.
questions.hint: Count up from c a semitone at a time, or take a perfect fourth and widen it.

questions.topic: The note that tells a French augmented sixth from the others
questions.learningObjective: identify the interval note that distinguishes the French augmented sixth
questions.stem: An augmented sixth in c major is spelled a-flat3, c4, d4 and f-sharp4, and it expands outward a semitone at each end to arrive on g. Why is this chord called the French sixth rather than the Italian or the German?

options.text: Because it contains d4, the second degree, instead of e-flat4, so the middle of the chord is a second above the tonic rather than its third
Because it has four notes like the German sixth, and the two four-note types are told apart only by the interval between a-flat3 and f-sharp4
options.misconception: believes the two four-note augmented sixths differ in their outer interval

options.text: Because it has four notes like the German sixth but resolves to the tonic rather than to the dominant
options.misconception: claims a different destination distinguishes the French from the German

options.text: Because it contains the tonic c4 and the second degree d4, whereas the Italian omits one of these two notes entirely
options.misconception: denies that the Italian sixth contains the tonic

questions.explanation: The three types are separated by what sits in the middle of the chord while the outer a-flat and f-sharp stay put and do their expanding. The Italian has only a-flat, c and f-sharp, so its middle note is the tonic. The German inserts the tonic's third, e-flat. The French inserts the second degree, d, so its middle is c and d a major second apart. That second is the useful part: it gives the French sixth a smoother connection to the dominant seventh that usually follows, because a chord built on the second degree is itself a predominant, and two predominants in a row move to the dominant with less strain than a predominant followed by a tonic-function chord. The trap is to sort the types by how many notes they have, which separates the Italian from the other two but cannot tell the German from the French.
questions.hint: All three keep the same outer notes, so compare the note in the middle of each chord.

questions.topic: Sizing the second inside a French augmented sixth
questions.learningObjective: compute the size in semitones of the second inside a French augmented sixth
questions.stem: A French augmented sixth in c major is spelled a-flat3, c4, d4 and f-sharp4. Counting semitones from c4 up to d4, how wide is the interval between those two inner notes?
questions.explanation: Up from c, c-sharp is one semitone and d is two, so c4 to d4 is a major second, two semitones wide. The second route is the same count read as a scale step: c and d are adjacent letter names, so the interval is some kind of second, and the only second worth two semitones is the major one, since a minor second would be a semitone. Two semitones matters in the chord because a-flat3, c4 and d4 already contain the notes of a supertonic triad, so the French sixth is a supertonic triad with the a-flat and the f-sharp laid over it. That is why it moves to the dominant so easily, and why the second is what a listener hears as the functional part of the chord. The trap is one semitone, which would require the note to be c-sharp rather than d.
questions.hint: Two adjacent letter names make a second, so the answer is one or two semitones.

questions.topic: The Neapolitan sixth and the function it serves
questions.learningObjective: state the function of a Neapolitan sixth and the motion that confirms it
questions.stem: In c minor a chord sounds d-flat3, f3 and a-flat3, holding a major triad in first inversion on the lowered second degree. What is this chord, and what does it do?

options.text: It is a Neapolitan sixth, and it works as a predominant, moving to the dominant so that the flattened second degree falls a semitone and the ear accepts a cadence in the minor
It is a Neapolitan sixth, and it works as a substitute tonic, so the passage can end on a-flat major instead of c minor
options.misconception: treats a predominant chord as a substitute for the final tonic

options.text: It is a flat supertonic triad in root position, and it works as a secondary dominant of g minor
options.misconception: names a first-inversion major triad as a root-position chord

options.text: It is an augmented sixth chord, and it works by expanding outward onto g, the same way an Italian sixth does
options.misconception: mistakes a first-inversion major triad for an augmented sixth

questions.explanation: The Neapolitan sixth is defined by three things at once: a major triad, a root a semitone above the tonic, and first inversion so that the lowered second degree is in the bass. In c minor that gives d-flat, f and a-flat with d-flat at the bottom, and the a-flat in the soprano above a bass d-flat is what makes the chord a sixth rather than a triad. Its job is to be a strong predominant, and the reason it is strong is that it lies only a semitone below the dominant: d-flat rises to d, the fifth of the dominant, or a-flat falls to g, the root, and either motion pulls hard towards g. Because the chord is a major triad it is bright, which is why it is used at the point in a minor-key movement where the music needs to lift before the cadence darkens again. The trap is to read the flattened second as a flat supertonic, which would be the same bass note with a minor third and a minor seventh above it instead of a major third.
questions.hint: Ask whether the bass is the lowered second degree, whether the triad is major, and what the chord is a whole step away from.

questions.topic: Sizing the third above the bass of a Neapolitan sixth
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval above the bass of a Neapolitan sixth chord
questions.stem: A Neapolitan sixth in c minor is spelled d-flat3, f3 and a-flat3 sounding together. Counting semitones from the bass note d-flat3 up to f3, how wide is the interval there?
questions.explanation: Up from d-flat, d-natural is one, e-flat two, e three, f four, so the interval from d-flat3 up to f3 is four semitones. The trap is three semitones, a minor third, which would make the chord a minor triad and turn it into the minor subdominant of c minor instead.
questions.hint: Name the interval from the letter names first, then count the semitones to confirm.

questions.topic: Why a diminished seventh chord can serve several keys
questions.learningObjective: explain why a diminished seventh chord is ambiguous and how it resolves
questions.stem: A chord spelled g-sharp4, b4, d5 and f5 appears in a piece without a key signature. It can lead to a minor, to c minor, or to e minor. What makes it fit all three, and what decides which?

options.text: It is a stack of three minor thirds and a diminished seventh, so any note of it can act as a leading tone to any of the four notes a semitone above it, and the bass and the resolution decide which key it means
It is a stack of three minor thirds, so all four of its notes are equally likely to be the leading tone and the composer must choose arbitrarily
options.misconception: denies that anything in the context favours one resolution

options.text: It fits all three keys because each of them uses the same three sharps, so the chord is simply a chord of the signature rather than of a key
options.misconception: confuses the key signature with the chord's set of pitches

options.text: It fits all three keys because a diminished seventh chord is never really in any key at all, so it cannot mislead a listener about the tonic
options.misconception: treats ambiguity as meaning the chord has no function

questions.explanation: Stack three minor thirds and you get four notes, and by the time you have the fourth note the span back to the first is a diminished seventh, nine semitones. The consequence is that every note in the chord has two neighbours a semitone away, one below and one above, and so every one of the four can be heard as a leading tone. A g-sharp is the leading tone of a, a b is the leading tone of c, a d is the leading tone of e, and an f is the leading tone of g, so this one chord can prepare four different tonics. Nothing in the chord itself decides, and that is exactly why diminished sevenths are so useful in a modulation: the composer can hold the chord while the bass moves, and the resolution names the key. The trap is to read the ambiguity as arbitrariness. It is not arbitrary, because a voice leading by step towards one of the four destinations is a strong signal, and so is the arrival of a bass that supports it.
questions.hint: Stack the chord in thirds and ask which note of it lies a semitone below which tonic.

questions.topic: The note that a common-tone diminished seventh shares
questions.learningObjective: identify the pitch a common-tone diminished seventh retains from the following chord
questions.stem: A chord spelled c4, e-flat4, g-flat4 and a4 sounds, and the next chord is the c major tonic triad c4, e4 and g4. What makes the first chord a common-tone diminished seventh rather than an ordinary leading-tone seventh?

options.text: It is built on the tonic c and that c is held over into the tonic triad, so the diminished seventh and the chord it resolves to share a note even though every other note changes
It is built on the tonic c, and building on the tonic is by itself enough to make any seventh chord a common-tone diminished seventh
options.misconception: assumes the root alone decides the chord type

options.text: It shares c4 with the following chord, and sharing any single note is what turns a leading-tone seventh into a common-tone diminished seventh
options.misconception: believes one common note alone is enough without the chord's own construction

options.text: It resolves to a major triad, and a diminished seventh that resolves upwards to a major triad is by that fact a common-tone diminished seventh
options.misconception: links the chord type to the quality of the chord it resolves to

questions.explanation: Two things have to be true at once, and this chord satisfies both. First, it is a diminished seventh: c to e-flat is a minor third, e-flat to g-flat is a minor third, g-flat to a is a minor third, and the span from c up to a is a diminished seventh of nine semitones, which is the interval pattern of the chord and the source of its four-way ambiguity. Second, its root is the tonic, and that root is the note it shares with the chord it resolves to, since the following triad is c, e, g and the c is held. So the ear hears a note that both prepares and belongs, and the remaining three notes can then move by step into e and g. The trap is to stop at the shared note, because sharing a note with the next chord is a description of what happens after the chord, not a name for the chord. A leading-tone seventh built on b would share nothing with the c major tonic and would have to resolve entirely by step.
questions.hint: Check both the interval pattern inside the chord and which note survives into the resolution.

questions.topic: The back-relating dominant and its late root
questions.learningObjective: describe how a third-inversion dominant seventh back-relates to a new key
questions.stem: A dominant seventh chord on g arrives in c major with its seventh f3 in the bass, and the g is held back in an upper voice until after the bass has moved. What makes this passage a back-relating dominant rather than a plain third-inversion chord?

options.text: The seventh in the bass points away from the chord's own key, so the f3 already behaves like a leading tone of b, and the g arriving late confirms that the music has turned towards e minor
The seventh in the bass is a chord member that has to resolve down, so putting it lowest guarantees a modulation whether or not one was intended
options.misconception: assumes the position of a chord member alone causes a modulation

options.text: The root is held back in an upper voice, so the chord is a dominant of the dominant and resolves to the dominant of g
options.misconception: names a secondary dominant where there is only a delayed root

options.text: The seventh in the bass makes the chord a leading-tone seventh, so the delayed g is simply a suspension above the same bass note
options.misconception: mistakes a seventh chord in third inversion for a suspension

questions.explanation: A dominant seventh in third inversion puts the seventh in the bass, and the seventh of g dominant is f. In c major f is nothing special, but a note a semitone below b is a leading tone to b, so the moment the seventh takes the lowest voice the bass has begun to point at b and therefore at e minor, the key of which b is the leading tone. The composer can then postpone the g itself, so the note that identifies the chord as a dominant arrives after the note that already suggests the new key. Hearing the f in the bass first and the g later is what produces the effect, and it is the delay, not the inversion, that is the point: a third-inversion dominant with its root sounding at once simply resolves to the second degree of its own key. The trap is to call it a dominant of the dominant, which would need a g chord with a raised third, and to call the delayed g a suspension, which would be a dissonance that has to resolve rather than a chord member arriving late.
questions.hint: Ask which key the note in the bass is a leading tone for, before the root has even sounded.

questions.topic: A pedal point and the chords that pass above it
questions.learningObjective: explain what a pedal point holds while the harmony above it changes
questions.stem: The bass sustains c2 for sixteen bars while the upper parts move through a6, d minor, g7 and a cadential six-four over the top of it. What is being held, and what is the effect of letting the harmony above it move?

options.text: The tonic c is being held as a pedal, and the changing chords above it are heard as a series of departures from and returns to that fixed point, which is what lets a long passage stay coherent
The bass note c is being held because the harmony above it has not changed, so the passage has no motion at all above the pedal
options.misconception: denies that the upper voices move while the bass is held

options.text: A dominant g is being held as a pedal, so the chords above it are first inversions of that one chord rather than separate harmonies
options.misconception: names a tonic pedal as a dominant pedal

options.text: The pedal is being held only to delay the tempo, so the changing chords above it are a harmonic decoration with no structural role
options.misconception: reduces a pedal point to a rhythmic device

questions.explanation: A pedal point is a single sustained or reiterated bass note under a changing harmonic series, and by far the commonest is the tonic. Its structural job is exactly what the other option denies: it supplies a fixed reference so that everything above it is measured against something. Six bars away from the tonic, a fourth away, a fifth away and back onto the tonic all acquire direction, because the bass has not moved to tell the ear that the harmony has. The chords themselves are not diminished by the pedal; a first-inversion tonic triad and a cadential six-four are heard for what they are, and the pedal only adds the knowledge of where the music is. The trick is that a pedal is not always the tonic. A dominant pedal sounds the same way and is usually reserved for the end of a movement, where a passage is closing and the dominant is what has to be reached.
questions.hint: Ask what the bass is doing while the upper parts move, and then what that tells the ear.

questions.topic: Counting the chords that are neither tonic nor dominant above a pedal

That accounts for four of the six, and the two left over are the 4 and the 6, a subdominant triad and a submediant triad, so the answer is two. The second route is simply to list the chords that survive: reading down the list 1, 4, 5, 1, 6, 5 and keeping only what is neither a 1 nor a 5 leaves the 4 and the 6, and there are two of them. Both are worth counting because they are what the pedal is holding in place while the harmony wanders, and if the passage consisted only of tonic and dominant chords the pedal would have nothing to organise. The trap is three, which counts the 6 once for each of the two tonic chords that surround it.

questions.topic: A cadential six-four and where it sits in the bar
questions.learningObjective: identify a cadential six-four by its bass and its metric position
questions.stem: In c major, on the second half of the second bar of a phrase, the notes sound g3, c4, e4 and g4, and the next chord is g3, b3, d4 and f4. What is the first chord, and why is it placed there?

options.text: It is a cadential six-four, a tonic triad with the dominant in the bass, and it is placed on the second half of the bar because that weak position keeps it sounding like a decoration of the dominant that follows
It is a tonic triad in first inversion, and it is placed on the second half of the bar because a first-inversion tonic is weak and belongs on a weak beat
options.misconception: reads the chord as an ordinary first-inversion tonic rather than a cadential one

options.text: It is a subdominant triad in second inversion, and it is placed on the second half of the bar because second-inversion triads are unstable
options.misconception: names the subdominant instead of the tonic triad

options.text: It is a dominant seventh in second inversion, and it is placed on the second half of the bar because the dominant is the strongest chord in the key
options.misconception: calls a tonic-triad sonority a dominant seventh

questions.explanation: The chord g, c, e is a c major triad with its fifth in the bass, so it is a six-four, and because the bass is the dominant note it is a cadential six-four rather than an ordinary tonic six-four. The metric position is the second half of the bar, and that is not incidental. A six-four is the least stable position a triad can occupy, with a fourth and a sixth stacked above its bass, so a composer who wants the ear to read it as part of what comes next rather than as an arrival puts it where the beat is weak. The following g, b, d, f is the dominant seventh, and the shared bass note g is what glues the two together, with the c falling to b and the e rising to f. A cadential six-four on a strong beat would sound like a genuine harmonic event, and in the earlier classical style it is precisely that kind of accent that tells a listener the dominant has arrived. The trap is the subdominant, which is a different root entirely.
questions.hint: Name the triad from its notes, then ask what the bass note is doing and how strong the beat is.

questions.topic: Sizing the fourth above the bass of a cadential six-four
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval above the bass of a cadential six-four chord
questions.stem: A cadential six-four in c major has g3 in the bass, with c4 and e4 above it. Counting semitones from the bass g3 up to the tonic c4, how wide is the interval the six-four is named for?
questions.explanation: Up from g, g-sharp is one, a two, a-sharp three, b four and c five, so the interval from g3 up to c4 is five semitones, a perfect fourth. The second route names it: g to c spans the letter names g, a, b, c, which is a fourth, and a perfect fourth is five semitones, so the name and the count agree. That fourth is one of the two intervals in the figured bass six-four, the other being the sixth from g up to e, and it is why the chord cannot stand on its own. The bass note g is the dominant of c, so the chord is a tonic triad standing on the dominant's note, and the fourth is what tells the ear that the tonic has not actually arrived. The trap is seven, which is a perfect fifth and is the interval from the bass to the note a fifth above it, not the fourth the chord is named for.
questions.hint: Name the interval from the letter names, then count the semitones to confirm it.

questions.topic: The Phrygian cadence and the bass note that makes it
questions.learningObjective: identify a Phrygian cadence by its chords and its half-step bass motion
questions.stem: In a minor, a progression runs f3, a3 and d4 over an f bass, then g-sharp3, b3 and e4 over a g-sharp bass. What kind of cadence is this, and what single feature defines it?

options.text: It is a Phrygian cadence, a first-inversion subdominant triad moving to a root-position dominant with the bass falling by a semitone from f to g-sharp
It is a plagal cadence, because the subdominant is moving to the dominant rather than the dominant to the tonic
options.misconception: calls a subdominant to dominant motion plagal

options.text: It is an authentic cadence, because the first chord is in first inversion and the second is a plain dominant triad
options.misconception: treats any two chords ending on the dominant as authentic

options.text: It is a half cadence in a minor key, and the semitone in the bass is simply the raised seventh degree doing its ordinary job
options.misconception: treats a Phrygian cadence as a plain half cadence

questions.explanation: The bass note is the whole of it. In a minor the subdominant triad is d, f, a, and putting the f in the bass gives a first-inversion subdominant, the figure usually written as a four six chord. The dominant is e, g-sharp, b in root position. So the bass travels f3 down to g-sharp3, and f to g-sharp is one semitone, the half step that gives the cadence its name. The effect is that the ear hears the leading tone arrive as a resolution, and a cadence that ends on a chord which is about to resolve is one that can be followed by a tonic without preparation. The trap is the plagal reading, which would require the bass to move a fourth or fifth downwards from the dominant to the tonic, and the trap of calling it a plain half cadence is that a half cadence could indeed end on the dominant, but it would not arrive there with the bass coming up by a semitone from the subdominant's third.
questions.hint: Look only at the bass line and ask how far it moves and in which direction.

questions.topic: Measuring the bass fall of a Phrygian cadence
questions.learningObjective: compute the semitone size of the bass motion in a Phrygian cadence
questions.stem: A Phrygian cadence in a minor has a subdominant triad in first inversion with f3 in the bass, moving to a root-position dominant with g-sharp3 in the bass. How many semitones does the bass fall?
questions.explanation: From f down to e is one semitone, and e is g-sharp's enharmonic equivalent, so the bass falls a single semitone. The second route measures it from above: f3 up to g-sharp3 is a whole tone of two semitones, and falling the same distance from f gives e, one semitone below f, which is the same pitch class as g-sharp. One semitone is the smallest possible interval and it is exactly what a Phrygian cadence is built on, because the bass arrives at the leading tone as though resolving rather than as though leaping. That is why the cadence can be followed immediately by a tonic and why it is used at the end of a phrase in a minor key where a full close would be premature. The trap is two, which is a whole tone and is what you would measure by rising from f to g-sharp instead of falling from f to its own octave.
questions.hint: Count the semitones downwards from the first bass note to the second.

questions.topic: What a half cadence leaves unresolved
questions.learningObjective: state what a half cadence does and which scale degree it ends on
questions.stem: A phrase in c major ends with a root-position g major triad and the melody resting on d, so the phrase stops without a tonic. What has happened, and what has been left open?

options.text: The phrase has made a half cadence on the dominant, and because the dominant triad is rooted on the fifth degree the tonic has not been confirmed, so the phrase is left waiting
The phrase has made a half cadence on the subdominant, because a root-position triad on g is the subdominant of c major
options.misconception: names the subdominant as the chord the phrase ends on

options.text: The phrase has made a full close, because a root-position triad is the strongest kind of chord and needs no tonic to follow it
options.misconception: believes root position alone makes a close conclusive

options.text: The phrase has made a half cadence on the tonic, because the melody resting on d shows that the tonic chord is implied underneath
options.misconception: reads an implied tonic underneath a dominant chord

questions.explanation: A half cadence is any cadence that stops on the dominant, and stopping on the dominant is by definition not settling, because the dominant's whole function is to pull towards the tonic and here that pull is never cashed. In c major the dominant triad is g, b, d, rooted on g, which is the fifth degree, so the phrase ends on scale degree five in the bass and the melody resting on d adds the fifth of the same chord above it. The effect is well suited to the middle of a movement, to the end of a first phrase, and to the end of a section that is about to continue, because it hands the listener a question instead of an answer. The trap is the subdominant, which in c major is f, a, c and not g at all, and the deeper trap is the assumption that a chord's position in the texture makes it conclusive. What makes a cadence conclusive is which chord it arrives on, not how that chord is voiced.
questions.hint: Ask which chord the phrase arrives on and which scale degree roots it.

questions.stem: A half cadence in c major ends on a root-position g major triad. Counting scale degrees upward from c in the c major scale, what number is g?
questions.explanation: The c major scale runs c, d, e, f, g, a, b, and counting from one gives c as one, d as two, e as three, f as four and g as five. The second route is functional: the scale degrees divide into tonic on one, predominant on four, dominant on five and tonic on one, and the chord a half cadence arrives on is by definition the dominant, which is five. Five is the answer that makes the cadence's name intelligible too, since the fifth degree is the one a half cadence sets up and then declines to resolve. The trap is four, which is the subdominant and the degree a plagal cadence would be measured against, or seven, which is the leading tone and a note rather than a degree on which a triad can rest.

questions.topic: The chord a deceptive cadence substitutes for the tonic
questions.learningObjective: identify the substituted chord and its scale degree in a deceptive cadence
questions.stem: A cadence in c major runs g3, b3, d4 and f4, then a3, c4 and e4, and the phrase ends there. Which degree has replaced the expected tonic, and why is the effect called deceptive?

options.text: The submediant, degree six, has replaced the tonic, so the ear was pulled towards a tonic by the dominant seventh and then given a chord a third away instead, which is why the close sounds like a swerve
The mediant, degree three, has replaced the tonic, so the ear was pulled towards a tonic by the dominant and then given the chord a fifth below it
options.misconception: names the third degree as the substitute

options.text: The subdominant, degree four, has replaced the tonic, so the ear was pulled towards a tonic and then given a chord that moves the wrong way entirely
options.misconception: names the fourth degree as the substitute

options.text: The supertonic, degree two, has replaced the tonic, so the dominant seventh simply failed to resolve and the phrase ended on the wrong chord by mistake
options.misconception: treats the effect as an error rather than a technique

questions.explanation: The dominant seventh g, b, d, f contains two notes that pull in opposite directions and both of them aim at the tonic: the b rises to c and the f falls to e. What a deceptive cadence does is deliver one of those resolutions and not the other, landing on a triad rooted on a, the sixth degree, which is built from c and e, the two notes the dominant seventh was aiming at. So the ear gets exactly what the dominant promised, a c and an e, and then has to place them in a different chord. The effect is a swerve rather than a stop, and that is why the technique is so effective at the end of a phrase: it uses the pull of the dominant to make the substitution sound inevitable. The trap is any answer that moves to a fourth or a fifth, because a chord a fourth above the dominant would be the tonic itself and a chord a fifth below would be the subdominant, neither of which is a swerve at all.
questions.hint: Find the root of the chord that arrives, count it as a scale degree, and check the notes it shares with the dominant.

questions.topic: The scale degree a deceptive cadence substitutes
questions.learningObjective: identify the scale degree substituted for the tonic in a deceptive cadence
questions.stem: A deceptive cadence in c major moves from a g7 chord to an a minor triad. Counting scale degrees upward from c, what number is the a that roots the substitute chord?
questions.explanation: The c major scale runs c, d, e, f, g, a, b, so counting upward a is the sixth degree, and the a minor triad built on it is therefore the submediant. The second route checks the substitution the same way the chord does: the dominant seventh g, b, d, f is aiming at c and e, and an a minor triad is a, c, e, so it delivers both of the notes the dominant was promising and simply places them in a different chord, a third above where the listener expected them. That third is the whole of the swerve, and a is a major third above c, which is four semitones, so the substitute sits four semitones from the tonic that was withheld. The trap is five, which is the dominant's own degree, and three, which would be the mediant and would not contain both c and e.

questions.topic: A plagal cadence inside a minor key
questions.learningObjective: describe a plagal cadence in a minor key and the notes it uses
questions.stem: A passage in c minor closes with d, f and a over a d bass, then c, e-flat and g over a c bass. What cadence is this, and why is it a little less available in a minor key than in a major one?

options.text: It is a plagal cadence, subdominant to tonic, and it is less crisp in a minor key because the subdominant's third is a minor third above the bass, so the top voice of the plagal chord lies a semitone below the tonic's third
It is a plagal cadence, and it is less crisp because a minor key has no subdominant triad at all, so the first chord has to be borrowed from the parallel major
options.misconception: denies that a minor key has a diatonic subdominant

options.text: It is an authentic cadence in a minor key, because the bass falls a fifth and a falling fifth is what an authentic cadence does
options.misconception: treats a falling fifth in the bass as an authentic cadence

options.text: It is a plagal cadence, and it is less crisp because the tonic triad in a minor key has a minor third, so the two chords share fewer notes than a major pair would
options.misconception: counts shared notes between the two chords as the reason

questions.explanation: A plagal cadence is the subdominant moving to the tonic, and here that is d, f, a to c, e-flat, g, with the bass falling from d to c a fourth or rising a fifth, which is what makes the bass move sound. The reason it is less crisp in a minor key is a small voice-leading fact with a large consequence. In a major key the subdominant's third, the third of the subdominant triad, sits a major third above the bass and a whole tone below the third of the tonic, so the leading tone of the plagal chord rises a whole tone to reach the tonic's third. In a minor key that subdominant third is f, a minor third above d, and the tonic's third is e-flat, a semitone below it, so the plagal chord's top voice has to fall. The consequence is that the plagal cadence cannot be prepared the way an authentic cadence is, which is one reason a minor-key piece tends to close on an authentic cadence or on a Picardy third instead. The trap is the denial that a minor key has a subdominant, which it certainly does.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that finds a pivot chord
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that decides whether a chord can pivot between two keys
questions.stem: Trace the rule pivot(a, b, chord), which returns yes when every note of chord lies in the scale of a and also in the scale of b, no otherwise, and in both cases returns the numeral of the chord's root counted in a and in b. With a equal to the c major scale, b equal to the a minor scale, and chord equal to a3, c4, e4, what does the rule return?

options.text: Yes, and the numerals are vi in c major and i in a minor, because a3, c4 and e4 lie in both scales and the chord changes only its name
No, because a minor triad is not a chord of the c major scale and so cannot belong to both keys at once
options.misconception: believes a minor triad can never be diatonic to a major key

options.text: Yes, but the numerals are VI in c major and I in a minor, because a numeral takes its case from the key rather than from the chord
options.misconception: assumes roman numerals take their case from the key signature

options.text: No, because the chord's root a is the tonic of one key only and a pivot chord has to be the tonic of both
options.misconception: requires a pivot chord to be the tonic of both keys

questions.explanation: Three of the seven notes of the c major scale and all seven of the a minor scale are shared, and a3, c4 and e4 are three of them, so the first test passes and the rule returns yes. The numerals then follow mechanically from the root: a is the sixth degree of c major, and a minor triad on the sixth degree is written with a lower-case numeral because the triad is minor, so vi; and a is the tonic of a minor, so the same chord is i. That the numeral changes while the chord does not is precisely what a pivot is. The trap in the second option is a real misunderstanding, since the c major scale does contain a natural minor triad on its sixth degree and that is where submediants come from. The third trap is the convention that decides the case: a lower-case numeral marks a minor or diminished triad, and a triad's quality is a property of the notes, not of the key it is being read in.
questions.hint: Check each note against both scales first, then count the root as a degree in each.

questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that reports the pitch classes two keys have in common
questions.stem: Trace the rule shared(a, b) = every note of the scale of a that also appears in the scale of b, in ascending order. With a equal to the c major scale and b equal to the g major scale, what does the rule return, and how many notes is that?

options.text: It returns c, d, e, g, a and b, which is six notes, because the g major scale adds f-sharp to the c major scale and changes nothing else
It returns c, d, e, f, g, a and b, which is seven notes, because c major and g major differ only in their key signatures

options.text: It returns c, d, e, f, g and a, which is six notes, because the note the g major scale drops is the leading tone of c major

options.text: It returns c, d, e, g, a, b and f-sharp, which is seven notes, because the union of the two scales counts as a shared collection
options.misconception: returns the union of two scales and calls it a common collection

Every other note survives, and the run c, d, e, g, a, b is six notes long. The fourth trap confuses a shared collection with a combined one, which would be a set of seven notes that belongs to neither key.

questions.stem: Trace the rule leading(key) = the note a semitone below the tonic of that key, and leading after the change when the music moves from c minor to e-flat major. What does the rule report for the new key, and what had it reported for the old one?

It reports d for the new key, replacing c, because the tonic itself becomes the leading tone once the key has changed

options.text: It reports f for the new key, replacing b-flat, because b-flat was a semitone below c in the minor key's natural form

options.text: It reports e-flat for the new key, replacing b natural, because the tonic is a semitone below itself once a new key is established

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that locates a pedal point
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that finds the longest run of chords sharing one bass note
questions.stem: Trace the rule pedal(chords) = the longest run of consecutive chords whose bass notes are all the same, and the rule is given the six chords of a c major passage with bass notes c, f, g, c, c and g. What does the rule return, and on which note?

options.text: A run of two chords on c, the tonic, since the two c bass notes are the only consecutive pair that repeats and no run is longer
A run of one chord on c, since no two neighbouring chords in the list share a bass note with the one before them
options.misconception: denies the adjacent pair of c bass notes in the list

options.text: A run of three chords on c, since c appears twice and must be counted once for each of its two appearances plus itself
options.misconception: counts repeated appearances of a note as consecutive chords

options.text: A run of two chords on g, since the g bass notes bookend the passage and are therefore the longest span available
options.misconception: treats non-adjacent chords as one consecutive run

questions.explanation: The rule only accepts neighbours, and the rule's own wording is what the distractors are built to violate. Reading the bass list c, f, g, c, c, g as runs gives one c, one f, one g, two c's, one g, and the longest of those is the two c's. That pair is a genuine pedal of two chords, and the c is the tonic, which is where pedals most often begin. The third option is the counting error the rule is designed to catch, since c occurs twice in the list and not three times, and only the second and third occurrences are adjacent. The fourth option is the error of ignoring adjacency altogether: the two g bass notes are at the third and sixth positions, with three chords between them, and a pedal has to be held under the harmony continuously or it is two separate pedal points. This is exactly why a pedal-point analysis is worth doing by hand rather than by counting appearances of a note.
questions.hint: Group the bass list into runs of identical adjacent notes and take the longest run.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that names a cadence from its arrival
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that classifies a cadence by the chord it arrives on
questions.stem: Trace the rule arrival(lastTwo) = the name of the cadence, chosen by the second of the two chords: a tonic triad gives a full close, a triad on the submediant gives a deceptive cadence, a triad on the dominant gives a half cadence, and anything else gives a plagal cadence. Applied to the last two chords of a phrase in c major, a g7 chord over g then an a minor triad over a, what does it return?

options.text: A deceptive cadence, since a minor is the triad on the submediant of c major and the second of the two chords is what the rule reads
A half cadence, since a dominant seventh is one of the two chords the rule was given and it looks for the dominant
options.misconception: reads the earlier chord instead of the one the rule is defined on

options.text: A full close, since the rule falls back to the tonic whenever a dominant seventh precedes, on the assumption that a dominant leads home
options.misconception: assumes a dominant seventh always resolves to the tonic

options.text: A plagal cadence, since anything the rule does not name explicitly is treated as a plagal close in a major key
options.misconception: sends every unrecognised arrival to the plagal category

questions.explanation: The rule keys on the second chord, so the first chord only tells you what the listener was expecting. The chord that actually arrives is a minor, a, c, e, and its root a is the sixth degree of c major, which is the submediant, so the rule returns a deceptive cadence. The dominant seventh before it is exactly the setup: its b and f were both aiming at c and e, and the a minor triad supplies c and e while placing them in a chord a third above where the listener expected to hear them. The second trap is the natural confusion of a two-chord description, where both chords are named and it is easy to read the rule as looking at the pair rather than at the arrival. The fourth trap shows why a classifier needs an explicit category for every possibility, since a catch-all rule will classify the commonest surprise in the language as something rare.
questions.hint: Ignore the first chord and ask only what arrived and what scale degree its root is.

questions.topic: Tracing semitone and letter steps in a descending sequence
questions.learningObjective: trace both the semitone and the letter step of a sequence bass
questions.stem: Trace two rules over a bass line. tone(notes) = the semitone difference between each pair of successive notes, and letter(notes) = the number of letter names each pair spans. Applied to the bass c4, a3, f3, d3, b2, g2, what do the two rules report together?

options.text: Tone gives minus three, minus four, minus three, minus three, minus four, and letter gives a third for every pair, so this is a diatonic sequence descending by thirds
Tone gives minus three, minus four, minus three, minus three, minus four, and letter gives a second for every pair, so this is a diatonic sequence descending by seconds
options.misconception: counts the letter span of a descending third as a second

options.text: Tone gives minus three at every step, and letter gives a third at every step, so this is a real sequence of descending minor thirds
options.misconception: assumes a diatonic third has one constant semitone size

options.text: Tone gives minus seven at every step, and letter gives a fifth at every step, so this is a real sequence of descending perfect fifths
options.misconception: reads a descending third as a descending fifth

questions.explanation: Running both rules is what stops the diatonic from being mistaken for the real. The letter rule settles the shape immediately: c to a spans the letter names c, b, a, which is a third, and so do a to f, f to d, d to b and b to g, so every step is a third and the sequence descends by thirds. The tone rule then shows why this is diatonic rather than real, because the steps are not all the same size: c4 to a3 is three semitones, a3 to f3 is four, f3 to d3 is three, d3 to b2 is three, and b2 to g2 is four. Alternating three and four semitones is what a diatonic scale does, since a diatonic third is a minor third going up from one scale degree and a major third from the next. A real sequence would hold one interval exactly, which is the fourth option, and that is a rule for descending fifths in the bass, not for thirds.
questions.hint: Count the letter names each pair spans before you trust any semitone figure.

questions.topic: The tonal answer to a fugue subject
questions.learningObjective: explain how a tonal answer differs from a real answer to a fugue subject
questions.stem: A fugue subject begins on c5 and rises to g5 before falling to e5. The second voice enters on g4 and rises to d5 before falling to b4. Why is this a tonal answer rather than a real answer?

options.text: Because the answer is transposed down a fifth to the dominant but its own intervals are adjusted to stay inside the new key, so the rise from g4 to d5 is wider than the original rise and the fall to b4 lands on the leading tone
Because the answer is a copy of the subject moved down a fifth with every note unchanged, so the two entries sound identical in shape and only in pitch
options.misconception: believes a real answer keeps every interval exactly as written

options.text: Because the answer is an exact inversion of the subject, so the rise becomes a fall and the listener is given the subject upside down
options.misconception: confuses a tonal answer with an inversion

options.text: Because the answer begins on the dominant rather than the tonic, which by itself is enough to make an answer tonal whatever happens to the intervals
options.misconception: reduces tonality to the starting note alone

questions.explanation: A real answer would move the subject down a fifth and change nothing else, so the rise from c5 to g5, a perfect fifth, would reappear as a rise from g4 to c5, a perfect fourth. That interval is a fourth above the dominant, and a fourth in that position is a dissonance in a fugue exposition, so a real answer is usable only when the subject's shape allows it. A tonal answer avoids the problem by adjusting the intervals, and here it has to: the rise from g4 up to d5 is a fifth, a tone wider than the original, and the fall from d5 to b4 is a third rather than a fourth. The point of the adjustment is that every note stays inside the key of the answer, so the answer sounds like the same idea re-aimed at the dominant rather than like a transposed scrap. The trap in the second option is the commonest misunderstanding of the whole subject, and the trap in the fourth is that a dominant entry is shared by real and tonal answers alike.
questions.hint: Compare the size of each interval in the answer with the size of the matching interval in the subject.

questions.topic: The interval that separates a subject from its tonal answer
questions.learningObjective: compute the interval between a subject's first note and its answer's first note
questions.stem: A fugue subject in c major begins on c5, and its tonal answer begins a fifth below on g4. Counting semitones from g4 up to c5, how wide is the gap between the two entries?
questions.explanation: Up from g4, g-sharp is one, a two, a-sharp three, b four and c five, so g4 to c5 is five semitones, a perfect fourth. The second route reads the same distance downward: c5 down to g4 is c, b, b-flat, a, a-sharp, g, six... reading it as a fifth from c5 down to g4 gives a perfect fourth below c5, and a perfect fourth is five semitones, which agrees. Five semitones is also what tells a listener that the second entry is the same idea in the other voice, since a fourth up from the dominant lands on the tonic, and the eye in the score is a fourth below the subject's opening note. The trap is seven, which is a perfect fifth and would be the distance measured from the subject's c5 up to the g5 an octave above, not between the two entries.
questions.hint: Count up a semitone at a time from the answer's first note to the subject's first note.

questions.topic: A circle-of-fifths sequence and the key it reaches
questions.learningObjective: describe how a circle-of-fifths sequence modulates and what its modulator is
questions.stem: A passage in c major runs through a sequence whose bass climbs by fifths from c through g, d, a and e, and the last chord of the sequence is a dominant seventh in the new key. What is happening, and what is the modulator?

options.text: The sequence is modulating by successive fifths towards a, and the modulator is the dominant seventh of a, because the root a is the fifth degree of the key the sequence has reached and the new key is confirmed when its own dominant arrives
The sequence is modulating by successive fifths towards a, and the modulator is the first chord of the sequence, because the first bass note is what fixes the starting key for the rest of the chain
options.misconception: names the opening chord of a sequence as its modulator

options.text: The sequence is a circle of fifths but it never modulates, because successive fifths return to the starting key and so the music is going in circles
options.misconception: assumes a closed circle of fifths means no modulation occurs

options.text: The sequence is modulating by successive fourths, and the modulator is the subdominant, because a bass climbing by fifths is the same motion as a bass falling by fourths
options.misconception: confuses the direction of the bass with the direction of the interval

questions.explanation: A chain of bass notes a fifth apart is the practical form of the circle of fifths, and because each step moves the key a fifth further round, four or five of these steps will land somewhere new. From c the chain goes to g, then d, then a, so after three steps the music is in a and the chords being heard are a's own diatonic chords. The word modulator names the single chord that makes this irreversible, and it is the dominant seventh of the arriving key, not the first chord of the chain. That is a useful distinction because the first chord only establishes where the sequence started, and a sequence can be abandoned halfway without the music having gone anywhere. The third trap is the real attraction of a closed circle, and it is worth being precise: the sequence returns to its starting pitch after twelve steps, not after three, and the point of the device is that a listener does not usually stay for twelve. The fourth trap is a true observation about the interval, a fifth up and a fourth down describe the same two notes, but the direction of the bass is what the ear follows.
questions.hint: Count the bass steps, work out which key each step reaches, and look for the chord that confirms the last one.

questions.topic: The signature reached by climbing successive fifths
questions.learningObjective: compute the key signature a chain of ascending fifths arrives at
questions.stem: A sequence climbs the circle of fifths from c major, and each successive bass note is a fifth above the last, so the chain runs c, g, d, a, e, b and f-sharp. How many sharps are in the key signature of the key the chain has reached?
questions.explanation: Each step of the chain is a fifth, and on the circle of fifths every fifth clockwise adds exactly one sharp, starting from none in c major. Counting along, c major has no sharps, g has one, d has two, a has three, e has four, b has five and f-sharp has six, so the key the chain reaches after six steps is f-sharp major with six sharps. The second route is to count the sharps the chain has added, one per step, and six steps have added six. Six is a great many sharps and the practical reason composers stop the chain well before this point is that the extreme keys become hard to read, so a passage that climbs four or five steps has usually already gone as far as is comfortable. The trap is one, which counts the first step only, or four, which is where a composer would sensibly stop rather than where a full six-step chain lands.
questions.hint: Count one sharp added per fifth and keep counting until you reach the end of the chain.

questions.topic: The bass fall across a sequence of descending thirds
questions.learningObjective: total the semitone descent of a diatonic sequence by thirds
questions.stem: A diatonic sequence in c major descends by thirds through the bass notes c4, a3, f3, d3, b2 and g2. Counting semitones downwards from the first note to the last, what is the total fall of the bass?
questions.explanation: Add the five steps one at a time. From c4 down to a3 is three semitones, a3 to f3 is four, f3 to d3 is three, d3 to b2 is three, and b2 to g2 is four, so the total is three plus four plus three plus three plus four, which is seventeen. The second route is to place the two end notes in one register: c4 sits at sixty semitones above the bottom of the keyboard's numbering and g2 at forty-three, and sixty less forty-three is seventeen. The alternation of threes and fours is the signature of a diatonic sequence, since a diatonic third is a minor third from one degree and a major third from the next, and it is why seventeen is not simply five times a single interval. The trap is fifteen, five steps of a minor third, which would be a real sequence and not a diatonic one.
questions.hint: Measure each of the five steps separately and add them, then check by subtracting the two end notes.

questions.topic: The pitch a sequence of descending sixths arrives at
questions.learningObjective: identify the pitch class a descending sequence of sixths arrives at
questions.stem: A diatonic sequence in c major descends by sixths through the bass notes c4, a3, f3, d3, b2 and g2, and then the seventh segment arrives at a single pitch. Counting pitch classes with c as zero, a as nine, e as four and f as five, what is the pitch class number of that seventh bass note?
questions.explanation: Descending by sixths is the same as ascending by thirds, so a chain that has run c, a, f, d, b, g continues to the note a sixth below g, which is the note a third above g, and a third above g in c major is b-flat, spelled as the sixth below. The last note of the given chain is g2, and the pitch class of g is seven, which is the number the question asks for. The second route is to note that the chain of thirds already supplied the answer: c is zero, a is nine, f is five, d is two, b is eleven and g is seven, so the pitch class of the arrival is simply seven, counted with c as zero and each sharp adding one. Seven is what distinguishes this answer from a reading of the interval: a sixth is nine semitones, and the question asks for a pitch class, not a distance. The trap is nine, which is a and therefore the second note of the chain rather than its last.
questions.hint: Pitch class numbers count semitones above c, so find the letter name first and then number it.

questions.topic: The pitch a real sequence arrives at
questions.learningObjective: compute the pitch a real sequence arrives at after several descending fifths
questions.stem: A real sequence in e-flat minor moves the bass down a perfect fifth at every step, starting on g4 and taking four such steps. Numbering the bottom octave of the keyboard as one, so that c4 is sixty and e-flat2 is thirty-nine, what number does the bass arrive at?
questions.explanation: A perfect fifth is seven semitones, so four descending fifths are twenty-eight semitones. The bass starts at g4, which is sixty-seven, and sixty-seven less twenty-eight is thirty-nine. The second route is to walk the chain note by note, checking each fifth: g4 at sixty-seven falls to d4 at sixty-two, which falls to a3 at fifty-seven, which falls to e3 at fifty-two, which falls to b2 at forty-seven... the fourth step is from e3 at fifty-two down to a2 at forty-five, so the chain reads sixty-seven, sixty-two, fifty-seven, fifty-two and then forty-five. Both routes must agree, and the disagreement here is a warning that one of them is wrong, which is exactly what happens when the number of steps is miscounted. Four descending fifths from g4 is a total of twenty-eight, and thirty-nine is a fourth below sixty-seven, while forty-five is only three steps. The trap is forty-five, which stops after three descending fifths instead of four.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of steps by seven semitones, then subtract from the starting number, and count the steps to check.

questions.topic: The pitch a chromatic sequence arrives at
questions.learningObjective: compute the pitch a chromatic sequence arrives at after several semitone steps
questions.stem: A chromatic sequence moves the bass down by one semitone at every step, starting on a4 and taking seven such steps. With c4 numbered sixty, so that a4 is sixty-nine, what number does the bass arrive at?
questions.explanation: Seven semitones below sixty-nine is sixty-two. The second route names the note as well as numbering it, which is worth doing because a sequence of semitones visits a mixture of letters. Walking down from a4: a4 at sixty-nine, a-flat4 at sixty-eight, g4 at sixty-seven, f-sharp4 at sixty-six, f4 at sixty-five, e4 at sixty-four, e-flat4 at sixty-three, and d4 at sixty-two. Seven steps lands on d4, and the fact that it lands on a letter a fourth above c4 is a coincidence of where the chain started, not a property of the device, since a chromatic sequence can start anywhere. The trap is sixty-one, which is a sixth below the start, and the more tempting error is to count the notes rather than the steps, which would give six because the starting note is the first of eight.
questions.hint: Subtract the number of semitones from the starting number, and then name the note to check.

questions.topic: The total span of a stretto's overlapping entries
questions.learningObjective: compute the span a stretto's overlapping entries occupy
questions.stem: A fugue subject lasts eight quarter notes, and four voices enter at quarter-note offsets of zero, three, six and nine, so that each entry begins before the previous one has finished. How many quarter notes elapse from the first entry to the end of the last?
questions.explanation: The first entry starts at zero and the fourth starts at nine, because the voices are spaced three quarter notes apart and the fourth is three spaces after the first, that is three times three. The fourth entry then lasts its full eight quarter notes, so the music runs from zero to nine plus eight, which is seventeen. The second route adds the three gaps to the length of one statement, three plus three plus three plus eight, which is the same seventeen arrived at from the other direction. Seventeen is also the best evidence that the entries really do overlap: if the last voice began at seventeen or later there would be no overlap at all, and a stretto in which the fourth entry waits until the third has finished is not a stretto. The trap is fifteen, which counts only the offsets and forgets the length of the final statement, and eight, which measures a single entry.
questions.hint: Find when the last voice enters, then add the length of one subject statement.

questions.topic: The total length of a repeated ground bass
questions.learningObjective: total the duration of a ground bass repeated a stated number of times
questions.stem: A passacaglia's ground is written as eight half notes, and the ground is stated twelve times in the movement with no shortening of the later statements. Measured in whole notes, how much music does the repeated ground occupy altogether?
questions.explanation: Eight half notes are four whole notes, since a whole note is two half notes and four halves make two wholes, so the ground itself is four whole notes long. Twelve statements of four whole notes each give forty-eight. The second route is to total in halves and then halve once at the end: eight half notes times twelve is ninety-six half notes, and ninety-six half notes are forty-eight whole notes. The fact that the later statements are not shortened is the point of the arithmetic, because in practice a composer almost always compresses the ground as the movement proceeds so that it can gather speed towards the end, and a movement in which twelve identical statements of four whole notes are played through unchanged would be very long. The trap is twenty-four, which is the total in half notes rather than whole notes.
questions.hint: Convert the ground into whole notes first, then multiply by the number of statements.

questions.topic: The distance from an old leading tone to a new one
questions.learningObjective: compute the distance between the leading tones of relative keys
questions.stem: A piece modulates from c minor to its relative major, e-flat major. The leading tone of c minor is b natural, and the leading tone of e-flat major is d natural. Counting semitones from b4 up to d5, how far apart are the two tendency tones?
questions.explanation: Up from b, c is one, c-sharp two and d three, so b4 to d5 is three semitones. The second route names the interval: b to d spans the letter names b, c, d, which is a third, and a third of three semitones is a minor third. Three semitones of real movement in a melody is the practical difficulty of a modulation to the relative major, because the two leading tones are not the same note respelled but two different notes a minor third apart, and the ear has to accept the loss of the old one before it can hear the new one. This is why the modulation is usually written so that the new leading tone arrives by step from some note that belonged to the old key. The trap is one, a semitone, which is what the new leading tone does at the cadence in its own key but not what it does on the way there.
questions.hint: Name the interval from the two letter names, then count the semitones to confirm it.

questions.topic: The distance from a diatonic seventh to an altered leading tone
questions.learningObjective: compute the distance from a key's seventh degree to a new key's leading tone
questions.stem: A piece modulates from e-flat major to its dominant, b-flat major. The seventh degree of e-flat major is d natural, and the leading tone of b-flat major is a-sharp. Counting semitones from d4 up to a-sharp4, how far apart are those two notes?
questions.explanation: Up from d, d-sharp is one, e two, f three, f-sharp four, g five, g-sharp six, a seven and a-sharp eight, so the distance is eight semitones. The second route names the interval: d to a spans the letter names d, e, f, g, a, which is a sixth, and a sixth of eight semitones is a minor sixth, so the name and the count agree. Eight semitones is a large move for a melodic line and it is the reason a modulation to the dominant is harder to disguise than one to the relative major, since the new leading tone is not a note that existed in the old key under another name. The note a-sharp has to be spelled and heard as an alteration, and the old seventh degree, d, has no further work to do once the new tonic arrives. The trap is five, a perfect fourth, which is what a d to g move would measure and which does not reach the a-sharp at all.
questions.hint: Name the interval from the letter names first, then count the semitones step by step.
