questions.topic: The notes a pivot chord shares with both keys
questions.learningObjective: count the pitch classes a common-chord modulation pivots on
questions.stem: A chorale modulates from c major to a minor on a chord spelled a3, c4 and e4. How many of the seven notes of the c major scale are sounded by that pivot chord?
questions.explanation: The chord sounds a, c and e, and all three of those notes belong to the c major scale, whose notes are c, d, e, f, g, a and b. So three of the seven are present. The second route counts the members of the chord rather than the members of the scale, which gives the same three: a chord is made of its notes, so a triad sounds exactly three of them whatever scale is being considered. Three is also the number that makes a common-chord modulation possible at all, since a chord built from notes common to both keys is simultaneously a chord of each, and a triad is the smallest such chord that can carry a function. The trap is four, which would be right for a seventh chord and wrong for a triad, and the trap of seven, which confuses the number of notes in a key with the number that a single chord can sound.
questions.hint: Count the notes in the chord, then check that each one is in the scale being left.

questions.topic: How long a regular phrase lasts at a stated tempo
questions.learningObjective: convert a regular phrase's measure count into seconds at a stated tempo
questions.stem: The antecedent of a period in common time is eight bars long, and the tempo is 120 quarter notes to the minute. How many seconds does the antecedent last?
questions.explanation: Common time has four quarter notes to the bar, so eight bars contain thirty-two quarter notes. At 120 to the minute a quarter note lasts half a second, because 120 is two per second, so thirty-two halves make sixteen seconds. The second route works in minutes and converts once at the end: thirty-two quarter notes at 120 to the minute is thirty-two over one hundred and twenty of a minute, and multiplying that by sixty gives sixteen seconds exactly. Sixteen seconds is worth noticing for what it implies, since it means a period's antecedent and consequent at this tempo come to about half a minute, and most phrases in this style occupy somewhere between four and eight seconds, so a sixteen-second phrase is a whole span of music rather than a small one. The trap is eight, which counts bars rather than quarter notes, and thirty-two, which is the count in quarter notes rather than the time in seconds.
questions.hint: Multiply the bars by the beats in a bar, divide by the beats per minute, and convert to seconds.

questions.topic: Reading a table of four modulations
questions.learningObjective: identify which row of a modulation table shows a pivot-chord change of key
questions.stem: A table lists four passages in c major with the chords each one reaches. Row 1 arrives on an e-flat major triad with no e-flat before it. Row 2 arrives on an a minor triad reached by way of a c major chord and then a d minor chord. Row 3 arrives on a g7 chord with its g in the bass. Row 4 arrives on a c major triad reached by way of an a minor triad. Which row shows a pivot-chord modulation, and what makes it different?

options.text: Row 4, because the a minor triad is a chord of c major and also the tonic of a minor, so the same three notes serve as the mediant of the old key and the tonic of the new one
Row 2, because it is the only row that passes through more than one chord before arriving, and a longer approach makes a modulation more securely a pivot
options.misconception: believes the length of the approach decides whether a pivot is involved

options.text: Row 1, because arriving on a chord with an e-flat means the e-flat has been introduced and so the key must have changed by a common chord
options.misconception: assumes a borrowed note is enough evidence of a pivot chord

options.text: Row 3, because a dominant seventh with its root in the bass is a pivot when the piece has already been in c major throughout
options.misconception: treats any dominant seventh as a pivot chord

questions.explanation: The test for a pivot is not how the music gets there but whether one chord belongs to both keys, and only row 4 satisfies it. Its a minor triad is the mediant of c major and the tonic of a minor, so a listener can hear either reading at the moment it sounds, and the following c major triad settles the second reading. The four other rows fail for four different reasons, which is what makes this table worth reading slowly. Row 1 arrives on a chord whose e-flat is foreign to the key, so nothing has been reinterpreted and the new key has simply been asserted. Row 2's approach is longer but every chord in it, c and d minor, is diatonic to c major, so it is a change of chord and not of key. Row 3 ends on the dominant, which is a half cadence and a deferral rather than an arrival anywhere. The trap in the second option is the one that catches experienced readers, since a long approach is often a sign of a carefully prepared modulation and can still contain no pivot at all.
questions.hint: Ask of each row whether the arriving chord could be read as a chord of the key that was left.

questions.topic: Reading a table of four cadences
questions.learningObjective: classify cadences from a table of chords and bass motion
questions.stem: A table gives the last two chords of four phrases. Row 1 is f3-a3-c4-f4 then g3-b3-d4-g4. Row 2 is f3-a3-d4 then g-sharp3-b3-e4. Row 3 is g3-b3-d4-f4 then a3-c4-e4. Row 4 is g3-b3-d4 then c3-e3-g3. Which row is a Phrygian cadence, and which single feature decides it?

options.text: Row 2, because the bass falls from f to g-sharp, a single semitone, and that half-step fall onto the leading tone is the whole definition of the cadence
Row 1, because its bass rises a fourth from f to g and a rising fourth is the motion a Phrygian cadence is built from
options.misconception: attaches the Phrygian cadence to a rising fourth in the bass

options.text: Row 3, because a deceptive cadence is a form of Phrygian cadence in which the tonic is replaced by the submediant
options.misconception: collapses the Phrygian cadence into the deceptive cadence

options.text: Row 4, because a plagal cadence and a Phrygian cadence differ only in whether the subdominant is in root position or first inversion
options.misconception: treats the two as a single cadence with two positions

questions.explanation: Only row 2 has the bass motion that defines the cadence, and the table is set up so that the other three rows are distinguished by the same test. Row 2's bass is f3, the third of the a minor subdominant triad, and then g-sharp3, the root of the dominant, so it falls by one semitone and the dominant is left with its leading tone in the bass. Row 1 rises a fourth from f to g, which is a plagal cadence read with the subdominant in first inversion, not a Phrygian one. Row 3 is the deceptive cadence, the dominant seventh moving to a triad a third above the tonic. Row 4 is a plain plagal cadence, g to c, the dominant moving to the tonic. The fourth trap shows the confusion worth naming: the Phrygian cadence is not a position of the plagal cadence, because in a plagal cadence the subdominant is in root position and the bass moves a fourth downwards, whereas here the subdominant is in first inversion and the bass moves upwards by a semitone onto a note that is not the tonic at all.
questions.hint: Compare the two bass notes in each row and look for a one-semitone fall onto a leading tone.

questions.topic: Reading a table of four sequences
questions.learningObjective: distinguish tonal from real sequences in a table of bass lines
questions.stem: A table gives the bass of four sequences, each with five segments. Row 1 is c4, a3, f3, d3, b2. Row 2 is c4, f3, b-flat2, e-flat2, a-flat2. Row 3 is c4, d3, e3, f-sharp3, g-sharp3. Row 4 is c4, c-sharp4, d4, d-sharp4, e4. Which rows are real sequences, and why?

options.text: Rows 2 and 4, because a real sequence copies one model segment at a fixed interval so that every segment has exactly the same intervals, and in row 2 every step is a descending perfect fifth while in row 4 every step is an ascending semitone
Rows 1 and 3, because a real sequence is one that descends diatonically, so the alternating thirds of row 1 and the rising steps of row 3 are both fixed-interval copies
options.misconception: confuses a descending diatonic chain with a fixed-interval copy

options.text: Rows 1 and 2, because both descend through the c major scale, so both keep one constant interval between their segments
options.misconception: judges a sequence by its key rather than by its intervals

options.text: Row 4 only, because a real sequence must ascend, since a descending bass cannot hold a fixed interval and still reach a new key
options.misconception: requires a real sequence to ascend and rules out descending fifths

questions.explanation: The whole distinction is whether the intervals repeat exactly, and the table is arranged so that each row fails or passes on that test for a different reason. Row 2's bass falls a perfect fifth at every step, since c to f is a fifth, f to b-flat is a fifth and b-flat to e-flat is a fifth, so the model segment is being copied at a fixed interval and the row is real. Row 4 rises a semitone at every step, and a semitone is a fixed interval just as much as a fifth, so row 4 is a real chromatic sequence. Row 1 descends by thirds, but a diatonic third is three semitones from one scale degree and four from the next, so the intervals are not constant and the row is tonal. Row 3 rises through consecutive scale steps and so likewise changes its interval size. The trap in the third option is worth flagging: descending through a scale is a good description of row 1 and no description at all of row 2, whose notes are not in one key once the accidentals appear.
questions.hint: Measure the interval between every pair of successive bass notes and see which row keeps one size throughout.

questions.topic: Reading a table of five phrase structures
questions.learningObjective: distinguish period, double period, sentence, hybrid and asymmetry from a table
questions.stem: A table describes five theme shapes. Row 1 is eight bars that end weakly and are answered by eight bars that end firmly on the tonic. Row 2 is sixteen bars made of two eight-bar units, each of which ends firmly on the tonic. Row 3 is sixteen bars whose first half presents four bars of melody over a steady accompaniment and whose second half continues with varied material before a firm close. Row 4 is eight bars of which the first two present the melody and the last six develop it. Row 5 is seven bars, grouped two then three then two. Which row is the sentence, and what makes it one?

options.text: Row 3, because a sentence divides into a presentation with its own continuation and then a continuation proper, and the firm close arrives only at the end of the whole sixteen bars
Row 1, because a sentence is an eight-bar unit with a weak first half and a strong second half, which is the definition of a period
options.misconception: confuses a period with a sentence

options.text: Row 4, because a sentence is an eight-bar unit that begins by stating a melody and then develops it, which is what row 4 describes
options.misconception: confuses a hybrid theme with a sentence

options.text: Row 5, because a sentence is defined by having uneven bar groups, so a seven-bar unit grouped two-three-two is the one that fits
options.misconception: judges a sentence by its metric irregularity

questions.explanation: The sentence is the theme shape that grows in two stages rather than answering a question, and the defining feature is that the arrival is postponed to the very end. Row 3 has exactly that: four bars of melody with a steady accompaniment and no cadence to stop the motion, then varied material that keeps the momentum going, and only in the last bars a firm close. That postponement is what distinguishes it from the period in row 1, where the first eight bars come to a proper cadential stop and the second eight bars answer them, and from the hybrid in row 4, where a two-bar presentation is followed by six bars of development inside a single eight-bar span. Row 2 is a double period, since each of its two halves is a complete eight-bar unit. The last trap catches a genuine feature of row 5, since seven bars grouped two-three-two is the standard way to write an asymmetrical phrase in simple time, but metric irregularity is not what makes a sentence a sentence.
questions.hint: Ask where the firm closing cadence falls and whether the first half comes to a stop of its own.

questions.topic: Reading a table of ground bass and stretto data
questions.learningObjective: interpret a table of entries and repetitions in two contrapuntal forms
questions.stem: A table gives two rows. Row 1 records a movement in which a bass of eight notes in half notes returns twelve times while a new melody is placed above it each time. Row 2 records a fugue whose subject lasts eight bars, with four voices entering at bars one, three, five and seven. Which row is a passacaglia and which is a stretto, and what single fact separates them?

options.text: Row 1 is the passacaglia, because a ground bass is a repeating bass with a new melody above it each time, and row 2 is the stretto, because the four entries at two-bar intervals overlap while the subject is still sounding
Row 1 is the stretto, because twelve returns of the bass compress the music, and row 2 is the passacaglia, because four voices over a repeating subject form a ground
options.misconception: swaps the two forms and misstates what each one repeats

options.text: Both rows describe the same procedure, because a repeating line with something new above it and overlapping entries are two names for one technique
options.misconception: treats a ground bass and a stretto as a single device

options.text: Row 1 is the passacaglia and row 2 is the chaconne, because a chaconne is identified by the number of voices entering rather than by the repetition of the bass
options.misconception: confuses a chaconne with a stretto and names the wrong criterion

questions.explanation: The two rows describe contrapuntal devices that work in opposite directions, and the fact that separates them is which element is the repeated one and whether the new material is above or beside it. In row 1 the bass is fixed and always returning, and the melody above it changes each time, so every statement is heard against a reference that has just been heard; that is a ground, and a ground stated many times with the melody above is what a passacaglia is. In row 2 the subject is the repeated element, and the four entries arrive at two-bar intervals while an eight-bar subject is still sounding, so no entry ever finishes before the next one begins and the texture tightens with each voice. The trap in the first option is a fair description of a compression effect, which is something a stretto does, but a bass returning twelve times is not itself a compression of the counterpoint. The last trap is worth correcting: the chaconne and the passacaglia are distinguished by the length and pattern of their grounds, and neither has anything to do with the number of fugue voices.
questions.hint: Ask of each row what is being repeated and whether the new material sits above it or arrives alongside it.

questions.topic: A structural claim the stated cadence contradicts
questions.learningObjective: reject a harmonic claim that the stated cadence cannot support
questions.stem: A commentary on a movement claims that its eight-bar opening is the first half of a period whose consequent will answer it. The opening is described as follows: the first four bars move c major, f major, g7 and c major, and the fifth to eighth bars move a minor, d minor, g7 and a root-position g major triad with the melody resting on d. Does the stated harmony support the claim?

options.text: No, because the opening arrives on a dominant triad and so closes with a half cadence, and a half cadence ends a first phrase rather than suspending one, so the eight bars are not antecedent and consequent of a single period
No, because the opening's first four bars already make a full close on the tonic, so the period would have been complete within the first four bars
options.misconception: reads the first four bars as the whole of a period on the strength of one tonic arrival

options.text: Yes, because the two halves are of equal length at four bars each, and equal length is what a period requires of its two phrases
options.misconception: believes equal phrase lengths alone make a period

options.text: Yes, because the presence of a dominant seventh in the second half prepares a cadence, and a prepared cadence can always be followed by the answering phrase
options.misconception: treats a prepared dominant as evidence that a consequent must follow

questions.explanation: The claim fails on the actual chords, and it is worth being exact about why. A period is two phrases of roughly equal length whose harmonic plans are parallel, with the first phrase cadencing weakly on the dominant and the second cadencing firmly on the tonic. The eight bars described do have two halves of four bars each, so the shape is right, but the fifth to eighth bars end on a root-position g major triad with the melody on d, which is a half cadence. A half cadence is a legitimate end to a first phrase, and the whole art of a period is that its first phrase is left open, so the comment has mistaken the end of the antecedent for a suspension of it. The two traps in the yes answers are both about shape rather than function. Equal length is necessary but not sufficient, since a sentence is also two halves of eight bars and is not a period, and a prepared dominant is what a half cadence consists of rather than evidence that something is still to come.
questions.hint: Look at the last chord of each half and ask whether it is a tonic or a dominant.

questions.topic: A ground bass and the melody that passes above it
questions.learningObjective: explain how a composer varies the harmony above a repeating ground
questions.stem: A movement in e minor is built on a ground bass of eight bars that returns many times while a different melody is heard over it on each statement. Explain what the ground supplies and what the composer has to keep changing.

answer.exemplar: A ground bass supplies a reference that never moves, and everything else in the music is measured against it. The eight bars of bass are heard again and again, and because they are heard again the ear builds an expectation about them: it knows where the ground begins, how long it lasts, and where the places are at which the harmony above it could change without the music losing its place. That is the real function of the device, and it is greater than the obvious one of providing harmonic support. The bass here is in e minor and it outlines the tonic triad, so every statement re-establishes the key as often as it is heard, which means the composer is free to wander a long way above it without the listener losing the thread. What the composer must then change is the melody. If the same melody were set above each return of the ground the piece would not be a passacaglia but a single tune with an accompaniment repeated under it, and it would become steadily more tedious rather than less, because the ear would anticipate both lines exactly. So each statement above the ground needs a fresh idea, and the fresh idea has to be harmonised so that the chords it implies are plausible above a bass that has not moved. This creates a productive difficulty. The bass supplies the harmonic floor, and the melody above is free to suggest chords of its own; the composer is then constantly negotiating between what the bass implies and what the upper parts imply, and a listener hears that negotiation as the music developing. The melody may also be related to the ground itself, taking its rhythm from the bass, which ties the two together without making the repetition dull. The wrong belief to avoid is that the ground bass is a form of accompaniment. It is closer to a rule that the music has to keep interesting itself inside, and the variation above it is not decoration but the actual subject of the piece.

questions.explanation: The question asks what the fixed bass gives and what the composer must keep changing, and the useful answer is that the ground is a reference rather than an accompaniment. Because it returns unchanged, the ear learns it, and every chord above it is then heard in relation to something known. The composer is therefore obliged to supply a new melody each time, since repeating the melody as well as the bass would produce a tune with a looped accompaniment rather than a ground-bass movement. The negotiation between the chords the bass implies and the chords the melody implies is what the listener hears as development, and it is also why melodies above a ground often borrow the ground's rhythm. The wrong belief to avoid is that the ground is decoration, when in fact it is the fixed term that makes the variation above it legible.
questions.hint: Ask what the fixed bass gives the ear, and then what would make the music stale.

questions.topic: A stretto and the compression it produces
questions.learningObjective: explain how overlapping entries in a stretto compress the texture
questions.stem: In a fugue, a subject lasting eight bars is entered by four voices at bars one, three, five and seven, so that each voice begins before the previous one has finished. Explain what this arrangement does to the texture and what it costs.

answer.exemplar: A stretto compresses the texture by overlapping the entries, and what it compresses first is the listener's ability to follow the material as separate lines. Taken one at a time, the four statements of the subject would be easy to hear: each voice enters on a recognisable figure, sings it through, and hands over. With the entries spaced only two bars apart against an eight-bar subject, six bars of the first voice are still sounding when the second begins and two bars of the second when the third begins, so at the height of the passage all four are sounding at once and all four are presenting the same figure. The effect is a thickening and an acceleration that has nothing to do with the tempo, since the pulse is unchanged and everything is heard to move faster. There is a second consequence, which is that the subject is heard as a single composite shape rather than as four statements, because the ear fuses the entries and follows the figuration through the whole texture instead of tracking one line. This is why a stretto is the traditional climax of a fugue exposition, and also why it cannot be sustained indefinitely. Once the entries are all in play the composer has exhausted the trick, and anything longer risks turning the passage into a drone with the melody buried inside it. The cost is legibility. Voices that are crossing, dissonances that are not being prepared, and a harmony that is being pulled in two directions are all much harder to control when the same material is sounding in every part at once, and the usual discipline is to write the stretto so that the first and last voices carry the shape clearly. The wrong belief to avoid is that a stretto is simply a faster fugue. The tempo never changes; what changes is the density, and density is heard as momentum.

questions.explanation: The arrangement changes what the listener can perceive rather than how fast it is played, since the pulse is untouched. Four entries two bars apart against an eight-bar subject mean that all four statements overlap, so the ear fuses them into one composite figuration and loses the ability to track a single voice. That fusion is the climax effect and also the limit, because once every voice is in play the device has nothing further to add and legibility becomes the problem. The wrong belief to avoid is that a stretto is a tempo device, when no note has changed value.
questions.hint: Ask what a listener can follow at once when four statements of the same material are sounding.

questions.topic: A phrase model and the harmonic skeleton under it
questions.learningObjective: describe the phrase model that underlies a melody and the harmony that supports it
questions.stem: A melody is built so that its first four notes are heard as the model and its later notes are recognised as repetitions of that model at different pitches. Explain what the model does, and how a harmonic skeleton underneath it helps.

answer.exemplar: A phrase model is a short figure that the melody quotes back to itself, and its purpose is to give a long melody the coherence of a short one without making it monotonous. The first four notes state the model, and everything afterwards is that model transposed, inverted, or shown at a different point in the scale, so a listener who has caught the opening recognises each return as related even though the pitches are new. What makes the model a phrase rather than a tune in the ordinary sense is that it is normally short, usually no more than a few notes, and that it is the unit of repetition rather than a decoration on top of a melody. The harmonic skeleton matters because the model is often disguised on its repetitions by the harmony underneath it, and if that harmony is not managed the listener may hear the repetitions as unrelated. A good skeleton does two things at once. It keeps the key stable enough that the transpositions of the model sound like the same idea in the same place, and it supplies a slow rhythm of change, often one chord to every two or four notes, so that the melodic repetitions land against different harmonies and therefore do not sound like a record skipping. The usual pattern is that the model is first stated alone over a simple bass, so that it is unmistakably present, and is then progressively combined with the harmony until the repetitions and the chords have become inseparable. By the time the melody closes, the listener has heard the model many times in different disguises, and the passage has the unity of a short figure without the brevity of one. The wrong belief to avoid is that a model is a refrain. A refrain comes back in the same form at the same pitch in every statement, whereas a model is expected to change, and its whole point is that it is recognisable while it is being altered.

questions.explanation: The model is a short figure the melody quotes back transposed or altered, and it is what lets a long melody sound coherent. The harmonic skeleton keeps the transpositions sounding like one idea in one key, and its slow chord rhythm stops the repetitions from sounding like a record skipping. The trap is calling a model a refrain, since a refrain returns unchanged at the same pitch while a model is meant to be recognisable precisely because it keeps changing.
questions.hint: Ask what the repetitions share, and what the harmony has to do with keeping the model audible.

questions.topic: A cadence avoided and the phrase that replaces it
questions.learningObjective: explain what a composer does when a cadence is withheld at a phrase ending
questions.stem: A movement reaches the end of a large section in e minor, sets up a dominant seventh that is plainly ready to resolve, and then moves to a first-inversion tonic triad with the melody suspended and the bass on the third. Instead of closing the section, the music continues. Explain what has happened and what takes the place of the cadence.

answer.exemplar: A cadence has been avoided, and the technique works by setting up an expectation so clearly that withholding the expected chord is itself an event. The dominant seventh in e minor is g-sharp, b, d and f, and its third and its seventh are both aimed at the tonic: the g-sharp rises to a and the f falls to e. A listener hearing the dominant has every reason to expect those two resolutions and a full close. What arrives instead is a first-inversion tonic triad, so the tonic does come, but in the least conclusive form available to it. There is no root in the bass, there is no arrival on a root-position chord, and the melody is suspended rather than settled, so the ear has received the destination without the closure. Two things are happening at once. The phrase has ended without a cadence, which is a legitimate and expressive choice, because a section that closes on an ambiguous chord leaves the music able to continue without a seam, and it has also strengthened the expectation for later, since a listener who has been refused a cadence once listens harder for the next one. What replaces the cadence is not a weaker version of the same event but a different kind of punctuation. Instead of a full stop the phrase receives a comma, and the harmony has to make that comma work: the first-inversion tonic is a chord that leans, and it usually leans onward, which is why the phrase that avoids a cadence almost always resolves its own internal tensions in a way that points forwards rather than backwards. The trick is that a composer cannot simply omit the dominant, because without the dominant there is no expectation to withhold and the avoidance means nothing. The device depends on the promise being made in full and then deliberately broken. The wrong belief to avoid is that avoiding a cadence is a failure of nerve. It is a positive decision, and a passage that ends its section on a root-position tonic simply cannot be given the same unsettled quality afterwards, whatever happens in the following section.

questions.explanation: The dominant seventh makes the expectation explicit and the first-inversion tonic frustrates it while still supplying the destination, so the phrase ends without closure. The device depends on the promise being made in full, since withholding a dominant that was never set up means nothing to the listener. The trap is treating avoidance as indecision, when it is a deliberate punctuation that leaves the section able to continue without a seam.
questions.hint: Ask what the dominant promised, what the listener was given instead, and how the phrase was allowed to end.

questions.topic: The order of events in a common-chord modulation
questions.learningObjective: rank the stages of a pivot-chord modulation in the order they occur
questions.stem: A chorale in c major modulates to a minor through a chord built on the note a. Put the five stages of the process into the order in which a listener must meet them.

options.text: The mediant triad of c major is established as a chord of the old key, then that same chord is heard with a new function, then chords diatonic to a minor follow, then the leading tone of a minor appears, and only then does the new tonic arrive in root position

The leading tone of a minor appears, then the new tonic arrives in root position, then the mediant triad of c major is established, then that same chord is heard with a new function, and finally the chords diatonic to a minor follow
options.misconception: begins with the arrival and the confirmation and only then sets up the old key

options.text: That same chord is heard with a new function, then the mediant triad of c major is established as a chord of the old key, then the new tonic arrives in root position, then the leading tone of a minor appears, and finally the chords diatonic to a minor follow
options.misconception: gives the new function before the old reading has been established

options.text: The chords diatonic to a minor follow, then the mediant triad of c major is established as a chord of the old key, then that same chord is heard with a new function, then the leading tone of a minor appears, and finally the new tonic arrives in root position
options.misconception: treats the confirmation of the new key as the last stage instead of the tonic itself

questions.explanation: The order is fixed by what a listener has to have already heard. First the a minor triad has to be an ordinary chord of c major, because until it is familiar as the mediant there is nothing for a reinterpretation to reinterpret. Second the same three notes have to be heard doing something else, and the sign that this has happened is usually a bass note or a melody note that belongs to a minor rather than to c major. Third the chords that are diatonic to a minor have to follow, so that the new key is populated before it is confirmed. Fourth the leading tone of a minor has to appear and be heard as a pull, since a tonic that has never been preceded by its leading tone does not register as a destination. Fifth the tonic arrives in root position, and only that gives closure. The distractor in the first option reverses the whole sequence, and the trap it exploits is real, since a reader looking at the score from the end sees the new tonic first and works backwards. The distractor in the second option swaps the second and first stages, which would be a modulation with no preparation. The distractor in the third puts the confirmation of the new key in the last place, but a leading tone and a closing cadence are two different things, and it is the tonic in root position, not the leading tone, that a listener experiences as having arrived.
questions.hint: Work out what must already be familiar before a chord can be reinterpreted, and what must be heard before a tonic can register as a destination.

questions.topic: The harmonic plan of a double period
questions.learningObjective: rank the four phrases of a double period by their cadences
questions.stem: A theme is a double period of sixteen bars made of four phrases of four bars, in d major. Phrase one cadences on the dominant, phrase two cadences on the dominant of the dominant, phrase three cadences firmly on the tonic, and phrase four cadences on the tonic. Put the four phrases in the order a double period requires.

options.text: The half cadence, the deceptive or evaded cadence, the authentic cadence, then the authentic cadence that closes the whole theme
The authentic cadence, the half cadence, the deceptive or evaded cadence, then the authentic cadence that closes the whole theme
options.misconception: opens the double period on a full close instead of a half cadence

options.text: The half cadence, the authentic cadence, the deceptive or evaded cadence, then the authentic cadence that closes the whole theme
options.misconception: places the first authentic cadence in the second phrase of the first half

options.text: The deceptive or evaded cadence, the half cadence, the authentic cadence, then the authentic cadence that closes the whole theme
options.misconception: puts the weaker cadence of the first half before the half cadence

questions.explanation: A double period is two periods, and the grammar is regular enough that the cadences can simply be listed. The first phrase ends with a half cadence, because a period's first half must not close. The second phrase ends with what is often called an evaded cadence, which may be a deceptive cadence on the submediant or a genuine avoidance, and this is the mark that distinguishes a double period from two separate periods, because the second half then begins to sound the way the first half did. The third phrase ends with a firm authentic cadence, closing the first of the two periods. The fourth ends with another authentic cadence, closing the theme, and the two closing cadences are usually at different structural levels so that the second is the more final. The distractor in the first option opens with an authentic cadence, which would mean the first phrase closed and there is no antecedent. The distractor in the second places the first authentic cadence in the second phrase of the first half, which destroys the parallel between the two halves. The distractor in the third is the one that sounds most plausible while being wrong, because the deceptive or evaded cadence in the second phrase is a weaker event than the half cadence that precedes it, and a period requires its first phrase to cadence the stronger of the two.
questions.hint: A double period is two periods, so decide which phrase ends the first period and which ends the theme.
